questions.prompt: Three parts are inspected in turn, and each passes (P) or fails (F). Which outcomes belong to the event "**exactly two** parts fail"? Choose every one.
questions.explanation: Exactly two failures and one pass: the pass can be first, second or third, so the event is {PFF, FPF, FFP}. FFF has three failures; PPF and FPP have one.

questions.prompt: A control panel has **four** relays, and each is either open or closed. How many outcomes does the sample space of the four relays' positions have?
questions.explanation: Each relay doubles the number of branches in the tree: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁴ = 16 outcomes, from all open to all closed.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is **9**? Give it to three decimals or more.
questions.explanation: Four of the 36 equally likely ordered pairs sum to 9: (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3). P = 4/36 = 0.1111.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "Two dice can sum to 2, 3, …, 12. That is 11 outcomes, so P(sum = 7) = 1/11." What is wrong?
options: The 11 sums are not equally likely; counting must use the 36 equally likely ordered pairs, which gives 6/36
The dice should be counted as one outcome, so there are 6 outcomes
questions.explanation: P(A) = favourable ÷ possible works only when every outcome is equally likely. A sum of 2 needs (1,1), one way, but a 7 can happen six ways. With the 36 ordered pairs, P(7) = 6/36 = 0.1667, not 1/11 = 0.0909.

questions.prompt: For one roll of a die, which pair of events is **mutually exclusive**?
options: A = "less than 4" and B = "an odd number"
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events share no outcome. {1} and {2, 4, 6} have nothing in common. The others overlap: 2 is in both of the second pair, 1 and 3 in the third, 3 and 4 in the fourth.

questions.prompt: A lab will test **4** of the **12** concrete cylinders cast on a pour. How many different groups of 4 can it choose?
questions.explanation: The order of choosing does not matter, so count combinations: C(12, 4) = 12! / (4! × 8!) = (12 × 11 × 10 × 9) / (4 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 11 880 / 24 = 495.

questions.prompt: A test rig has three slots, first, second and third, and **3** of **6** sensors are to be placed in them. How many different arrangements are there?
questions.explanation: The slots are in order, so order matters: permutations, 6P3 = 6 × 5 × 4 = 120. Combinations, C(6, 3) = 20, would count only which three sensors are used.

questions.prompt: A box of **12** fuses holds **3** blown ones. A technician takes **2** fuses at random. What is the probability that **both are good**? Give it to three decimals or more.
questions.explanation: Every pair is equally likely: C(12, 2) = 66 pairs. Pairs of good fuses come from the 9 good ones: C(9, 2) = 36. P = 36/66 = 0.5455.
